c.tagline: Japan's industrious third city — castles, carmakers, and miso-rich comfort food.

taxi.fareNote: Ride-hailing apps (GO, Uber, DiDi) only dispatch licensed, metered taxis rather than private cars; plentiful street and rank taxis are all metered.

avoid.reason: In the Sakae and Nishiki nightlife districts, ignore bar touts late at night to avoid overcharging scams.

hood_desc: Nagoya's buzzing central entertainment and shopping district, home to the Nagoya TV Tower, the Oasis 21 'spaceship' park, department stores and the city's densest cluster of bars, izakaya and clubs. The best base for nightlife and downtown energy.

The soaring skyscraper district around JR Nagoya Station — JR Central Towers, Midland Square and the Dai Nagoya Building — packed with hotels, underground malls and unbeatable rail links, including the Shinkansen. Ideal for first-timers who want maximum convenience.

A lively warren of covered shopping arcades around the Osu Kannon temple, mixing vintage clothing, electronics, otaku subculture and cheap street food. Suits younger travelers and bargain-hunters after an eclectic, local buzz.

The historic and civic heart north of downtown, anchored by the reconstructed Nagoya Castle with its golden shachi and the greenery of Meijo Park, alongside offices and quieter streets. Great for sightseeing and a calmer stay near the sights.

A major rail interchange south of the center with well-priced business hotels and easy access to the airport train, the port and downtown. A practical, low-key base for travelers who value connections over flash.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout Japan.

transit.pay: Buy a manaca IC card at station machines, tap a nationwide Suica/ICOCA, or use a contactless bank card; base subway fares start around ¥210 (~$1.40). manaca gives discounted transfers between the subway and city buses.
transit.hours: The subway and trains run roughly 5:30am to just past midnight; night buses and taxis fill the gap after the last trains.

food.name: Hitsumabushi
food.desc: Grilled eel over rice in a lacquered box, eaten in three stages: plain, with condiments, then as chazuke with hot dashi poured over.

places.name: Atsuta Horaiken Honten
places.note: Serving hitsumabushi since 1873 and holder of the trademark; expect a wait.

places.name: Maruya Honten
places.note: Reliable branch inside the station complex, ideal before a shinkansen.

places.name: Ibasho
places.note: Century-old eel house in a wooden townhouse; lunch sets are better value.

food.name: Miso katsu
food.desc: Deep-fried pork cutlet under a thick, glossy sauce of dark Hatcho miso instead of the usual tonkatsu sauce.

places.name: Yabaton Yabacho Honten
places.note: The 1947 original; order the waraji katsu, a cutlet the size of a sandal.

places.name: Yabaton Esca
places.note: Underground-mall branch with shorter queues than the main shop.

places.name: Osu Shopping Arcade
places.note: Several long-established miso katsu counters along the covered arcade.

food.name: Tebasaki
food.desc: Nagoya-style chicken wings, twice-fried without batter then brushed with a sweet-salty glaze and a heavy hit of black pepper.

places.name: Sekai no Yamachan
places.note: Peppery wings and cheap beer; the flagship izakaya of the Nagoya chain.

places.name: Furaibou
places.note: The sweeter, stickier rival style; branches across the station area.

places.name: Torikai Sohonke
places.note: Chicken specialist using Nagoya Cochin birds for a meatier wing.

food.name: Miso nikomi udon
food.desc: Chewy, hard-boiled udon stewed in a clay pot of dark red miso broth with chicken, spring onion and a cracked egg.

places.name: Yamamotoya Sohonke
places.note: The best-known name for the dish; noodles stay deliberately firm.

places.name: Yamamotoya Honten
places.note: Separate old house of the same tradition, popular with office workers.

places.name: Nikomi no Takara
places.note: Small arcade shop favoured by locals for a lighter, homier broth.

food.name: Kishimen
food.desc: Flat, ribbon-wide wheat noodles in a clear bonito broth, topped with fried tofu, spinach and drifts of shaved katsuobushi.

places.name: Miya Kishimen Jingu-ten
places.note: Open-air tables inside the shrine forest; a Nagoya rite of passage.

places.name: Yoshida Kishimen
places.note: Esca-mall stalwart, quick and dependable between trains.

food.name: Taiwan ramen
food.desc: A Nagoya invention despite the name: soy broth loaded with fiery chilli-garlic minced pork, chives and bean sprouts.

places.name: Misen Imaike Honten
places.note: The shop that created the dish in the 1970s; ask for it milder if unsure.

places.name: Misen Nagoya Station
places.note: Same recipe in a handier location for travellers.

food.name: Kissaten coffee and morning service
food.desc: Nagoya's cafe culture throws in toast and a boiled egg free with morning coffee, often with sweet ogura red-bean paste on the side.

places.name: Komeda's Coffee
places.note: Homegrown Nagoya chain; the classic morning set with shiro noir dessert.

places.name: Kako Coffee
places.note: Hand-drip specialist famous for its ogura toast breakfast.

places.name: Osu Shopping Arcade cafes
places.note: Cluster of old-school kissaten still running morning service.

food.name: Nishio matcha
food.desc: Aichi's Nishio district is one of Japan's great matcha regions, and Nagoya cafes serve it as lattes, floats and dense gelato.

places.name: Nanaya Sakae
places.note: Graded matcha drinks and gelato from level one to an intense level seven.

places.name: Osu Kannon tea shops
places.note: Tea merchants around the temple pour matcha to drink in or take away.

landmarks: Nagoya Castle
Twin golden shachihoko dolphins crown the reconstructed keep of Ieyasu's mighty 1612 fortress, beside the lavishly restored Honmaru Palace's gilded screens.
Atsuta Jingū
One of Shinto's holiest shrines, sheltering the sacred sword of the imperial regalia within a serene forest of thousand-year-old camphor trees.
Ōsu Kannon and Ōsu Shopping District
A vermilion Buddhist temple opens onto kilometer-long covered arcades mixing vintage fashion, electronics, street food, and pop culture.
Toyota Commemorative Museum of Industry and Technology
In Toyota's original red-brick loom works, live demonstrations trace the company's evolution from textile machinery to world-conquering automobiles.
SCMAGLEV and Railway Park
JR Central's spectacular train museum lines up shinkansen record-setters and the 603-km/h maglev alongside Japan's largest railway diorama.
Oasis 21 and Chubu Electric MIRAI Tower
A floating glass 'Spaceship-Aqua' roof and Japan's first TV tower light up the Sakae district, dazzling on evening strolls.
Nagoya City Science Museum
Its gigantic silver globe houses one of the world's largest planetariums, plus deep-freeze and tornado labs beloved by families.
Tokugawa Art Museum and Tokugawaen
Heirlooms of the Owari Tokugawa lords, including Genji scrolls and samurai armor, adjoin a graceful strolling garden of ponds and peonies.
Port of Nagoya Public Aquarium
One of Japan's largest aquariums stages orca and dolphin performances and recreates marine habitats from Japan's seas to Antarctica.
Shirotori Garden
Nagoya's largest Japanese garden sculpts a miniature Kiso River landscape with teahouses, ideal for matcha beside carp-filled ponds.

train.note: Japan has no international trains. Nagoya is a Tokaido Shinkansen hub: bullet trains reach Tokyo in about 1 hour 40 minutes and Shin-Osaka in about 50 minutes - book on smartEX in English. The Shinano limited express runs north to Matsumoto and Nagano, and the Hida express to Takayama. Meitetsu and Kintetsu private lines fan out across central Japan and to Ise and Nara, often cheaper than JR, and Meitetsu also runs the airport train to Centrair.

bus.note: No international buses run from Japan. Long-distance and overnight highway buses leave the Meitetsu Bus Center at Nagoya Station for Tokyo, Kyoto, Osaka, Kanazawa, Takayama and Hiroshima - the main operators are Willer Express (https://willerexpress.com/en/) and JR Tokai Bus. Overnight coaches to Tokyo take about 6 hours and cost far less than the Shinkansen; Willer sells online in English while JR Bus seats are bought at the centre or on the Japanese booking sites.

intl.to: Sendai & Tomakomai, Hokkaido (Japan) - sails from Nagoya Port, about 25 min by subway from the centre

ferry.note: There are no international ferries from Nagoya. The Taiheiyo Ferry sails from Nagoya Port every other day on a scenic domestic long-haul, reaching Sendai overnight and Tomakomai in Hokkaido about 40 hours after departure, with cabins, a restaurant and a bath on board. It is one of Japan's most enjoyable ferry rides and cabins sell out in summer, so book well ahead, especially with a car.

half.name: Inuyama
half.blurb: A castle town 30 minutes north with Japan's oldest original wooden keep and the Meiji-mura open-air architecture museum nearby.

half.name: Toyota City
half.blurb: Home of the Toyota Kaikan showcase and factory tours, plus the automobile museum — the beating heart of Japan's car industry.

half.name: Gifu
half.blurb: See cormorant fishing on the Nagara River below Gifu Castle, about 20 minutes away by train.

full.name: Ise
full.blurb: Ise Grand Shrine, Shinto's holiest site, with the nostalgic Okage-yokocho streets — about 1h30 by Kintetsu limited express.

full.name: Takayama
full.blurb: A beautifully preserved Edo-era old town in the Hida mountains, reachable in about 2h20 by the Hida limited express.

full.name: Magome & Tsumago
full.blurb: Walk the cobbled Nakasendo post road between two restored Kiso Valley post towns.
